reasoning: ق glottalises even in this learned word. Educated Ramallah speakers keep ث here, though sa'aafe with s is also heard; taa marbuta after ف is e.
Literally on the hand of the left. ش is a sun letter so the article assimilates, ish-shmaal; left is shmaal with the short vowel dropped, as against shamaal for north.
kull plus shi run together. Many Ramallah speakers pull them apart again as kull ishi, which is just as common.
First person past with the dialect's initial cluster, nja7t. Palestinians keep the full imti7aan, not the Egyptian im7aan, and say nja7 bi- rather than fi-.
Brand name used as the generic word for instant coffee; the final vowel is long ee and the written ه is silent.
ظ is the emphatic interdental, written TH; the shadda doubles the n. baTHunn aah is a hedged yes; baftikir is an equally common alternative.
A written-register adjective that keeps [q]; it turns up in phrases like ma'aal qayyim but not in Ramallah conversation. Speakers say ghaali, or ilo 'iime kbiire for something of value.
Used in everyday talk about tadfi'a markaziyye, central heating. The medial hamza is written ', and the final vowel comes out a after it.
One syllable with no case ending. The identically spelt noun sahl 'plain' is a separate sense.

romanization: ya ghaayib 3an il-3een ya ghaayib 3an il-'alb
vowelled_arabic: يَا غَايِب عَن العِين يَا غَايِب عَن القَلْب
reasoning: ق in 'alb is a glottal stop; ع and ق are both moon letters so the article stays il-. The more usual wording of the same proverb is il-bi3iid 3an il-3een bi3iid 3an il-'alb.
3imil is the Palestinian past of to do, not 3amal. The English phrase is borrowed whole; the Arabic term laqTet shaasha is not used in speech.
ث in thaanye is pronounced t, so the Arabic is respelt تَانْيِة. The phrase introduces a contrast, so on the other hand is closer than from another perspective.
Both ض are emphatic, written D; the shadda doubles the m in Damm. News vocabulary that is entirely ordinary in Ramallah conversation.
The normal Palestinian word for one's grandfather, used as both address and reference. Long ii in the first syllable.
Condolence formula. ص is emphatic S; ق in y'awwiik is a glottal stop, with the shadda doubling the w.
From nashshaf, to dry. The nsh sequence is n followed by ش. Taa marbuta after ف is e.
miin is the Palestinian who; ma kaan generalises it to whoever, on the pattern of ween ma kaan and keef ma kaan.
Long oo; taa marbuta after ج is e. Genuinely used, though in casual Ramallah speech a man more often says marti or il-mara.
shloon belongs to Gulf, Iraqi and Hourani-Syrian speech; it is understood in Ramallah but never said there. The Palestinian word is keef.
A written-style connector; said aloud the taa marbuta comes out -e, natiije la-. In conversation a Ramallah speaker says bisabab or 3ashaan.
ث is pronounced t, so thawb is toob and the Arabic is respelt تُوب. ط is emphatic T, and the shadda doubles the r. This is the embroidered Palestinian dress.
The ma...-sh circumfix is alive in Palestinian and adds emphasis over plain ma shufto. shuft plus the -o object gives shuftoo- before the -sh.
Italian borrowing, collective; one tomato is banadooraaye. Taa marbuta after ر is a.
A fixed news and political term, so ق tends to keep [q] here even for speakers who glottalise elsewhere. ط is emphatic T; taa marbuta after ز is e.
Long ii then a short final o. Used for both the weight and, in other contexts, the kilometre.
